title: Introduction to Classes and Objects
summary: Class is the type and access boundary; object is independent heap state plus identity. Design choice is where you draw the boundary and what you hide.

refs.title: Classes and Objects in Java - GeeksforGeeks
Understand Classes & Objects in 8 Minutes - YouTube

blocks.title: The one idea that matters
blocks.text: A **class is a type that decides what state can exist and who is allowed to touch it**. An **object is one isolated chunk of that state with its own identity on the heap**. If your design does not give each object independent state behind a controlled boundary, you do not have objects — you have a struct with functions.

A class is a user-defined type. It declares three things: the shape of state (fields), the allowed operations on that state (methods), and the rules for creating valid state (constructors). It also declares the access boundary: which members are part of the contract and which are implementation detail. The class itself holds no per-instance data. It is a compile-time template plus method code shared by all instances. The trade-off is made here: you pay upfront definition cost and boilerplate to gain compiler-checked structure and a single place to enforce invariants.

An object is an instance of that type, and every useful object has three properties. **State** is the current values in its fields. **Behavior** is what its methods can do with that state. **Identity** is what distinguishes this instance from another instance with identical field values. Two `Dog` objects both named `Tuffy` aged 5 are not the same dog if they are two allocations — `==` on references tells you that, `equals` on values does not. The trade-off: identity plus owned state gives you isolation and reasoning power, but every object costs a heap allocation, header overhead, and reference indirection versus a flat primitive.

blocks.title: From class definition to living object
blocks.caption: Class code is shared; state is per-object on the heap; the variable holds only identity.
blocks.code:
flowchart TD
  ClassDef[Class definition - fields plus methods] --> NewOp[new plus constructor]
  NewOp --> HeapObj[Heap object - own state]
  NewOp --> StackRef[Stack reference - identity]
  StackRef --> MethodCall[Method call on reference]
  HeapObj --> MethodCall
  MethodCall --> HeapObj

blocks.text: Nothing exists until three steps happen. **Declaration** like `Dog tuffy;` creates only a reference slot, initially null. No object, no memory for fields, no invariant. **Allocation** with `new` reserves heap memory for the fields plus object header and yields an identity. **Initialization** runs the constructor, which must take the raw memory from an invalid to a valid state. Skip this discipline and you get the classic production bug: a non-null reference pointing at default-zeroed state that violates every assumption. Constructor enforcement is the trade-off: mandatory parameters make invalid objects unrepresentable, but they make deserialization, testing, and frameworks harder because every creation path must supply the full valid state.

The memory model is why aliasing surprises juniors. The variable `a` lives on the stack or inside another object and holds only a reference — a pointer to identity. The fields `name`, `breed`, `age` live on the heap inside the object. Assignment `Dog b = a;` copies the reference, not the object, so `b.age = 6` mutates the same heap cell `a` sees. `new` is the only thing that gives you fresh independent state. The trade-off is fundamental: reference semantics make passing large objects cheap because you copy 8 bytes, but they make reasoning about who mutated what expensive because any holder of the reference can mutate shared heap state.
The access boundary is the design

Fields should be private by default and exposed only through intentional methods. Not because privacy is virtuous, but because every public field doubles as an uncontrolled write API that no invariant can survive. If `age` is public, nothing stops `-40`. If `age` is private and mutated only through `haveBirthday()` or a validated setter, the class can guarantee `age >= 0` forever and change internal representation — `int age` to `LocalDate birthDate` — without breaking callers. The trade-off: encapsulation buys you freedom to refactor and enforce rules, but you pay in boilerplate and in the temptation to add a getter for everything, which re-exposes the field and deletes the benefit you just paid for.

`static` fields and methods belong to the class, not to any instance. There is exactly one copy shared by every object. Use it for true class-level facts: constants, instance counters, factories. Never use it for per-request or per-entity state, because you have just created global mutable state wearing object-oriented syntax. The trade-off is brutal: static is convenient and allocation-free, which is why novices overuse it, but it destroys isolation, makes tests order-dependent, and breaks the moment two threads or two tenants need different values. If you are writing `static int age` inside `Dog`, you have one age for all dogs. That is never what you meant.

blocks.caption: Honest trade-offs of the class-object model
rows: Class with private fields + behavior
Invariants enforced in one place; safe refactoring
More code; must design the method surface carefully
Public fields / record-style holder
Less boilerplate; easy construction and debugging
No control over mutation; invariants leak to every caller
Heap object per entity
Independent state + identity; aliasing is explicit
Allocation + GC pressure; indirection cost vs primitives
Constructor validation
Invalid states unrepresentable; fail fast at creation
Rigid creation; harder for mappers, tests, and partial builds
Inheritance for reuse
Shared code with polymorphic substitution
Fragile base class; hidden coupling; prefer composition

blocks.text: Classes fail in four predictable ways. First, the **anemic object**: private fields with dumb getters and setters and all logic in a manager elsewhere. You paid for encapsulation and got a struct. Invariants live nowhere. Second, the **god object**: one class that knows about persistence, validation, formatting, and networking because it was convenient to add one more method. Changes collide and tests need the whole world. Third, **leaked representation**: returning a mutable internal list or date directly, so callers mutate your private state without calling you. Fourth, **aliasing plus null**: storing a passed-in mutable reference without copying it, or dereferencing a declared-but-never-initialized reference. The trade-off in every case is short-term velocity versus long-term containment. Skipping the boundary ships faster this sprint and charges interest on every later change.

items: `NullPointerException` on a freshly declared reference: symptom is a crash on the first method call because declaration is not instantiation — `Dog d; d.getAge()` never allocated.
State corrupts silently across callers: symptom is one request overwriting another because two variables alias the same heap object or share a `static` field.
Invariant violation at a distance: symptom is `age = -1` in the database because a public field or unvalidated setter bypassed the constructor check.
Defensive-copy bug: symptom is a caller mutating the list you returned from `getOrders()` and your internal state changes without any log line inside your class.
Constructor does real work (I/O, threading, statics): symptom is slow startup, flaky tests, and objects that are half-built when construction throws midway.

blocks.title: Aliasing is the exam trap
blocks.text: Passing an object passes its identity, not a copy. If your constructor stores the caller's list directly, you share fate. Copy mutable inputs in, copy mutable outputs out — or document shared ownership explicitly. The trade-off: copying costs CPU and memory but buys isolation; sharing is fast but requires a protocol for who may mutate.
How it shows up in the interview

items.title: Define it without reciting a textbook
items.text: Say class as type plus boundary, object as identity plus owned heap state. Then point at `int` vs `1` or `Dog` vs `new Dog(...)` to show even built-ins follow the same rule.

items.title: Write the two-instance proof
items.text: Create two objects with identical values, show `==` is false, mutate one, show the other is unchanged. This proves you understand identity versus equality and heap independence.

items.title: Harden one field
items.text: Take a public field, make it private, add constructor validation and one behavior method instead of a setter. Narrate the trade-off: boilerplate now for invariant safety forever.

items.title: Draw the memory split
items.text: Sketch stack reference versus heap object and walk through `Dog b = a` versus `new Dog(a)`. Interviewers promote on this distinction more than on syntax.

items.title: Defend composition over inheritance
items.text: When asked to extend, prefer embedding a collaborator over subclassing. Explain why: inheritance couples you to base-class internals; composition keeps the boundary explicit at the cost of one more field.

items: Class and object are synonyms: no — class is the definition and shares code; object is the allocated instance with its own state and identity.
Declaring a variable creates an object: no — `Dog d;` is a null reference. Only `new` plus a constructor brings an object into existence.
Objects live where variables live: no — variables hold references on the stack; non-primitive objects live on the heap and are reached through those references.
Private means secure: no — it means contained. Reflection and same-class code can still reach it. The goal is a small, changeable interface, not security.
More getters mean more encapsulation: backwards — every trivial getter re-exposes representation. Expose behavior (`haveBirthday()`) not raw state.
Static fields give each object its own copy: backwards — static is one copy for the class. Per-object state must be instance fields.

blocks.caption: When a class earns its place — and when it does not
rows: Entity has identity + lifecycle: Customer, Order, Dog
Value is defined purely by contents: use immutable value holder
Invariant must hold across mutations: age non-negative
No invariant and no behavior: plain data carrier is clearer
Multiple instances need isolated state with shared behavior
Only one instance ever exists with global config: consider explicit singleton scope, not statics scattered everywhere
Behavior varies by type and needs polymorphism
Behavior is a single function: a function or strategy interface avoids a hierarchy

blocks.title: What to say in one sentence if asked
blocks.text: A **class defines the state shape, allowed operations, and access boundary as a type; an object is one independently mutable instance of that type with its own identity on the heap** — so design the boundary to enforce invariants, not just to hold data.
